United States v. Windsor. In June 2013, the Supreme Court ruled five to four to strike down the federal portion of the Defense of Marriage Act, or DOMA, which had denied federal benefits to same-sex married couples. Justice Kennedy wrote the majority opinion, establishing that DOMA violated equal protection and represented a major step toward full marriage equality. The case involved Edith Windsor, who sought a federal estate tax refund after her wife Thea Spyer died. DOMA had categorically denied that refund to her, revealing how the statute harmed surviving same-sex spouses in concrete ways across hundreds of federal programs. Kennedy's majority held that DOMA violated the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause and expressed an improper disapproval of same-sex marriage. The decision invalidated Section Three of DOMA, which had defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman for federal purposes. It struck down DOMA's denial of federal tax benefits, Social Security, and other spousal protections to legally married same-sex couples. However, the decision left in place state-level DOMA definitions, setting the stage for Obergefell two years later to address marriage bans themselves. Justice Scalia's dissent warned that the ruling would inexorably lead to nationwide same-sex marriage, a prediction that proved accurate when Obergefell was decided in 2015.
